ar_perim.title: Area vs perimeter
ar_perim.explanationHTML: Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape (add the sides). Area is the space inside it (for a rectangle, length × width). They are different measurements with different units (cm vs cm²).
ar_perim.workedExample: A 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle: perimeter = 6+4+6+4 = 20 cm, but area = 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

ar_add.title: Area is multiply, not add
ar_add.explanationHTML: For a rectangle, area = length × width. Adding the two sides gives you half the perimeter, not the area.

tr_nohalf.title: Triangles need the ½
tr_nohalf.explanationHTML: A triangle is exactly half of the rectangle around it, so area = ½ × base × height. Forgetting the ÷ 2 doubles your answer.

tr_add.title: Triangle area: multiply, then halve
tr_add.explanationHTML: Use ½ × base × height — multiply the base and height, then halve. Adding base + height is not area.

vc_add.title: Volume multiplies three lengths
vc_add.explanationHTML: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height (cm³). Adding the three edges gives a length, not a volume.

vc_sa.title: Volume vs surface area
vc_sa.explanationHTML: Volume is the space inside (l × w × h, in cm³). Surface area is the total of all 6 faces (in cm²). The question word — 'fits inside' vs 'covers' — tells you which.
vc_sa.workedExample: 2×3×4 cuboid: volume = 24 cm³; surface area = 2(6+8+12) = 52 cm².

vc_face.title: A cuboid has all three dimensions
vc_face.explanationHTML: Multiplying only two edges gives the area of one face. Volume needs all three edges multiplied together.
vc_face.workedExample: 5 × 3 is a face (15 cm²); 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³ is the volume.

mn_sum.title: Mean: don't forget to divide
mn_sum.explanationHTML: The mean is the total ÷ how many numbers there are. The sum on its own is not the mean.

mn_div.title: Divide by how many numbers
mn_div.explanationHTML: For the mean, divide the total by the count of values — not one less. Five numbers means ÷ 5.

mn_count.title: The mean is a value, not the count
mn_count.explanationHTML: How many numbers there are is the count. The mean is total ÷ count — a different thing.

me_mean.title: Median is the middle, not the mean
me_mean.explanationHTML: The median is the middle value once the numbers are in order. The mean (add up, divide) is usually different.

me_max.title: Median is the middle, not the largest
me_max.explanationHTML: Put the numbers in order and take the one in the middle. The biggest number is the maximum, not the median.

me_unsorted.title: Sort before you take the middle
me_unsorted.explanationHTML: The median is the middle value after sorting. Taking the middle of the unsorted list gives the wrong number.

rg_add.title: Range is a subtraction
rg_add.explanationHTML: Range = largest − smallest. It measures the spread, so you subtract — never add.

rg_max.title: Range is the gap, not the biggest
rg_max.explanationHTML: The range is how far apart the values are: largest − smallest, not the largest value itself.

pb_wrong_total.title: Probability is out of the TOTAL
pb_wrong_total.explanationHTML: Probability = wanted outcomes ÷ total outcomes. The denominator is every item, not just the others.

pb_red.title: Answer the colour that was asked
pb_red.explanationHTML: Check which outcome the question wants. Working out a different colour's probability is a common slip.
pb_red.workedExample: Asked for blue with 2 blue of 10 → P(blue) = 2/10 = 1/5.

fw_wrong_base.title: ‘Of what is left’ uses the new amount
fw_wrong_base.explanationHTML: After spending some, the next fraction is taken from what remains, not from the original total. Work one step at a time.
fw_wrong_base.workedExample: £24, spend 1/3 → £8 gone, £16 left. Then 1/4 of £16 = £4, so £12 left.

fw_stop.title: Finish every step
fw_stop.explanationHTML: Multi-step problems aren't done after the first step. Re-read what is asked and carry the working all the way to the end.
fw_stop.workedExample: £24 → after 1/3 spent, £16 left → after 1/4 of that spent, £12 left (the final answer).

fw_spent.title: Spent vs left
fw_spent.explanationHTML: Read carefully whether the question wants how much was spent or how much is left — they are different numbers.
fw_spent.workedExample: Spent £8 of £24 → £8 is spent, but £16 is what's left.

Number.title: Slow down on number work
Number.explanationHTML: Most number slips are misreading the question or a careless step. Underline exactly what is asked, work one step at a time, and check the size of your answer makes sense.
Number.workedExample: Estimate first: 412 − 187 should be about 400 − 200 = 200, so an answer of 225 is sensible, 595 is not.

Reasoning.title: Turn words into a clear plan
Reasoning.explanationHTML: For ratio, algebra and sequences, write down what each part or letter stands for before calculating. Find the value of one part first, then build the rest.

Measurement.title: Check the units first
Measurement.explanationHTML: Before adding or subtracting, make sure everything is in the same unit (all cm, or all minutes). Mixed units cause most measurement mistakes.
Measurement.workedExample: 3 m − 145 cm → make both cm: 300 − 145 = 155 cm.

Geometry.title: Name the property you're using
Geometry.explanationHTML: Angle problems rely on a fact (angles on a line = 180°, in a triangle = 180°, round a point = 360°). State the fact, then form the calculation.

Data.title: Mean, median, mode, range — pick the right one
Data.explanationHTML: Each average answers a different question: mean = total ÷ count, median = middle (sorted), mode = most common, range = largest − smallest. Match the word in the question to the method.
